title: Seven mana, four windows, one telegraphed wrath: tap out for the double engine, or hold the metronome open?

board.you: Turn 5, precombat main. Battlefield: Radagast of Rhosgobel (2/5, cast turn 4 — dead on his 4.01 goldfish average), Llanowar Elves (untapped), Wood Elves (1/1), and six untapped Forests — five land drops plus the Forest Wood Elves fetched. Seven mana available counting the Elves. Hand: Ohran Frostfang, Beast Whisperer, Indrik Stomphowler, Heroic Intervention. You are at 38.
board.table: Player 2 (token aggro, at 34) has nine 1/1s under an anthem enchantment; her attacks have gone at Player 4 two turns running, and she swings wherever the blocks look worst. Player 3 (Azorius control, at 36) holds five cards, drew two extra last turn, and passes with exactly four mana untapped — stated archetypal assumption: a sorcery-speed wrath in hand and the patience to time it. Player 4 (ramp midrange, at 29) is tapped out under a big mana engine. The table read Radagast's textbox when he landed; nobody has attacked you yet.

scenario.question: Do you tap out for the double engine — Beast Whisperer discounted to {G}{G}, then Ohran Frostfang at retail — hold all seven and deploy only at flash speed across the three opponent turns, or split: Whisperer on your main, the rest held?

branches.choice: Tap out: Beast Whisperer discounted, Ohran Frostfang at retail
branches.line: Main phase: cast Beast Whisperer as your turn's first creature spell — Radagast prices it {G}{G}. Then cast Ohran Frostfang at its full {3}{G}{G}, because the discount is spent: only the first creature spell each turn gets it (stack 001's bound). Seven mana, two engine pieces, pass with nothing open.
branches.signals: Sorcery-speed engine assembly is the loudest thing this deck can do. The table watches a draw engine and a deathtouch anthem land in one turn and re-files you from developing seat to setting-up seat — and Player 3 is holding the exact card that punishes whoever the table just agreed on.
branches.coalition_risk: High. You volunteer as the wrath's reason with zero mana to answer it, and the token player redirects her next swing at the seat that just showed ambition and can no longer pay for Heroic Intervention.
branches.coaching: Run the arithmetic before you fall for this line. These same two bodies cost seven tapped out and five through the windows — the discount resets every turn, so the tap-out is the only sequencing that pays retail. Now price the exposure: both pieces stand through Player 3's turn with Heroic Intervention uncastable, into four open mana and two extra cards. That is overextending into a telegraphed sweeper for nothing — a flashed body attacks on turn 6 just the same, and a 2/3 and a 2/6 block one token each. The only real purchase is Whisperer triggers one rotation early, and a swept engine triggers nothing. Keep the two mana and the table's respect.

citations.quote: The total cost is the mana cost or alternative cost (as determined in rule 601.2b), plus all additional costs and cost increases, and minus all cost reductions.
don't overextend into an unknown sweeper without a reason; commit exactly as much as wins before it arrives, no further

branches.choice: Hold all seven: deploy only through the flash windows
branches.line: Attack with nobody, pass with seven up. Then work the windows — one discounted creature per turn, every turn, per stack 001. If Player 2 sends tokens your way, flash Indrik Stomphowler ({2}{G} discounted) after attackers are declared — a 4/4 blocker whose arrival smashes the anthem, shrinking every attacker back to a 1/1. Flash Beast Whisperer ({G}{G}) on Player 3's end step, once they pass with the wrath unspent — their window closed, yours opened. Flash Ohran Frostfang ({1}{G}{G}) on Player 4's end step, drawing a card off the Whisperer already on board. Both attack on your turn 6 exactly as if you had tapped out today. Keep {1}{G} for Heroic Intervention the whole way round.
branches.signals: Seven open mana from the Radagast seat is a sentence the whole table reads three times. Every attack gets priced against a possible ambush, every wrath against a possible save — and you have not spent a card. Bodies that appear only on end steps never give the sweeper player a snapshot worth four mana.
branches.coalition_risk: Lowest at the table. You are the seat nobody can profitably attack and nobody can justify wrathing — the deflection posture the strategic frame prescribes, held for one more round.
branches.coaching: This is the deck, so play it like you mean it. The table believes open mana is a bluff you will eventually stop affording — prove them wrong four windows a round. Stack 001 is your license: the discount-plus-flash resets on every player's turn, so held bodies are cheaper than deployed ones and lose zero attack tempo. Sequencing is the discipline — Whisperer before Frostfang so the second cast draws, always after the scary turn's window closes, never more than the turn needs. And know your own clock: you sit at three bodies against a pivot bar of five, holding the overrun by turn 6 only 42.4% of the time — so this turn's job is not committing, it is making three opponents play worse while you draw toward the commit. The card they cannot see is doing more work than any card you could show them.

citations.quote: If a spell would have flash only if certain conditions are met, its controller may begin to cast that spell as though it had flash if those conditions are met.
“Flash” means “You may play this card any time you could cast an instant.”
A creature can’t attack unless it has been under its controller’s control continuously since their most recent turn began.
Leaving instant-speed mana open forces three players, not one, to respect your possible interaction.

branches.choice: Split: Beast Whisperer on your main, hold five
branches.line: Main phase: Beast Whisperer for {G}{G} — your own turn's window would otherwise expire unused. Pass with five: Ohran Frostfang ({1}{G}{G} discounted) for the best flash window, {1}{G} reserved for Heroic Intervention.
branches.signals: One modest engine piece at sorcery speed with five still up: you read as a developing seat with teeth. But Player 3 logs the draw engine, and a wrath that catches Whisperer plus your dorks now trades up against you.
branches.coalition_risk: Moderate. Whisperer alone rarely makes you the archenemy, but it hands the wrath a reason — and forces an ugly choice when it comes: spend Heroic Intervention saving a two-mana creature, or eat the loss.
branches.coaching: Right rhythm, wrong turn. On a quiet board this split is the deck's standard round — the engine at half price on your main, the traps armed behind it. This turn has a telegraphed wrath in it, and the split walks Whisperer into it for the price of impatience: one opponent turn of earlier triggers. Worse, it points Heroic Intervention at the wrong job. That card is the pivot-turn insurance — held for the turn you commit five bodies and a finisher, not a seatbelt for a 2/3. Waiting one end step buys the same Whisperer, after the wrath window closes, with the Intervention still aimed at the turn that wins. File the split for the round Player 3 taps out.

citations.quote: hold the protection spell for the turn you commit, not after

recommendation.choice: Hold all seven: deploy only through the flash windows
recommendation.rationale: The wrath is telegraphed and the pivot bar is not met — three bodies against five, the overrun in hand 42.4% by turn 6 — so nothing deployed at sorcery speed today wins the game, and everything held taxes three opponents at once. Stack 001 makes the patience free: the window recurs on every player's turn, held bodies come down discounted on end steps, and they attack on schedule anyway. The tap-out pays two extra mana for the privilege of being wrathed; the split donates the engine one turn early. Hold the seven. The threat of the unknown card is the deck.
